title: Ἀγαμέμνονος ἐπίδρομος
about: Agamemnon takes the two sons of Antimachus alive in their chariot, whose reins have slipped from their hands. They beg for ransom from their father’s stores, but Agamemnon recalls how Antimachus urged the Trojans to kill Menelaus when he came to ask for Helen, and he kills them both. The Achaeans press the Trojans back across the plain like a fire in woodland, Zeus draws Hector out of the dust and blood, and the Trojans run past the tomb of Ilus to the Scaean Gates. Agamemnon strikes down the hindmost like a lion among cattle. As he nears the wall, Zeus sits on Ida and sends Iris to tell Hector to keep out of the fighting until Agamemnon is wounded; Hector leaps down, rallies his men, and the lines meet. The poet then calls on the Muses to say who first stood against Agamemnon.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ Πείσανδρόν τε καὶ Ἱππόλοχον μενεχάρμην
υἱέας Ἀντιμάχοιο δαΐφρονος,
sentences.l:
But he — Peisander and Hippolochus, steadfast in the fray,
sons of Antimachus, wise-minded,
sentences.i: As for Peisander and Hippolochus, steadfast in the fray, the sons of wise-hearted Antimachus,
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὃ ‘but he’ is Agamemnon, as lines 126 and 129–130 show, but no verb follows: the accusatives Πείσανδρον and Ἱππόλοχον stand as the topic, and the sentence starts again at 126 with τοῦ … δύο παῖδε ‘of him … two sons’, where Agamemnon’s act comes. μενεχάρμην is singular, so it goes with the nearer name, Hippolochus; it is the stock epithet ‘steadfast in the fray’ (μένω ‘stand fast’ + χάρμη ‘fight’). υἱέας is the epic accusative plural of υἱός. δαΐφρονος is ‘wise-minded’ in `l` and ‘wise-hearted’ in `i`; whether it means ‘wise’ or ‘fierce’ is disputed. The unit stops at the comma, in the middle of line 123.

sentences.t:
ὅς ῥα μάλιστα
χρυσὸν Ἀλεξάνδροιο δεδεγμένος ἀγλαὰ δῶρα
οὐκ εἴασχ’ Ἑλένην δόμεναι ξανθῷ Μενελάῳ,
sentences.l:
who most of all,
gold, of Alexander, having received, splendid gifts,
kept not allowing Helen to be given to fair-haired Menelaus,
sentences.i: who, most of all, having accepted gold from Alexander, splendid gifts, kept refusing to let Helen be given to fair-haired Menelaus,
sentences.n: ὅς ῥα μάλιστα ‘who most of all’ opens a relative clause on Antimachus. δεδεγμένος is the perfect participle of δέχομαι ‘receive, accept’; χρυσόν ‘gold’ and ἀγλαὰ δῶρα ‘splendid gifts’ stand side by side, the second naming what the first was. Ἀλεξάνδροιο has the epic genitive -οιο (= Attic -ου); Alexander is the other name of Paris. εἴασχ’ is εἴασκε, the imperfect of ἐάω ‘allow’ with the iterative suffix -σκ-: he refused not once but every time the matter came up, hence ‘kept refusing’ in `i`. δόμεναι is the epic infinitive of δίδωμι ‘give’. ξανθῷ Μενελάῳ is the stock ‘fair-haired Menelaus’.

sentences.t:
τοῦ περ δὴ δύο παῖδε λάβε κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
εἰν ἑνὶ δίφρῳ ἐόντας, ὁμοῦ δ’ ἔχον ὠκέας ἵππους·
sentences.l:
of him indeed two sons took lord Agamemnon
in one chariot being, and together they held the swift horses;
sentences.i: lord Agamemnon caught two sons of his, who were in one chariot, and together they were driving the swift horses;
sentences.n: τοῦ ‘of him’ is Antimachus, picked up again with περ δή after the long relative clause. δύο παῖδε is a dual, ‘two sons’, the two named in 122–123; λάβε is the unaugmented aorist of λαμβάνω ‘take hold of, seize’. κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων is the stock ‘lord Agamemnon’. ἐόντας is the epic participle of εἰμί (= ὄντας), ‘being’, and εἰν ἑνί is ἐν ἑνί ‘in one’. ἔχον is a plural, ‘they held’, for the two together; ὠκέας ἵππους ‘swift horses’ with ἔχον ‘drove’ in `i`, as at 3.263. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
ἐκ γάρ σφεας χειρῶν φύγον ἡνία σιγαλόεντα,
τὼ δὲ κυκηθήτην·
sentences.l:
for out of them, from the hands, escaped the glossy reins,
and the two were thrown into confusion;
sentences.i: for the glossy reins slipped out of their hands, and the two were thrown into confusion;
sentences.n: ἐκ γάρ … φύγον ‘for … escaped’ gives the reason the brothers are helpless. σφεας is the epic accusative ‘them’, set beside χειρῶν ‘from the hands’ in the way Greek names a person and then the part: ‘out of them, from the hands’. φύγον is the aorist of φεύγω, with ἡνία σιγαλόεντα ‘the glossy reins’ as its subject (σιγαλόεις is the house ‘glossy’). τὼ δέ ‘and the two’ is a dual article used as a pronoun, and κυκηθήτην a dual aorist passive of κυκάω ‘stir up, throw into confusion’. The unit stops at the raised dot, in line 129.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἐναντίον ὦρτο λέων ὣς
Ἀτρεΐδης·
sentences.l:
and he, against them, rushed like a lion,
Atreus’-son;
sentences.i: and the son of Atreus rushed at them like a lion;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is Agamemnon, named by Ἀτρεΐδης at the start of the next line, which is why the unit carries on one word into it. ὦρτο is an aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’ in the middle, ‘rose, rushed’. ἐναντίον ‘against (them)’; λέων ὣς ‘like a lion’, with ὣς placed after its noun. Ἀτρεΐδης ‘son of Atreus’ stands for Agamemnon. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of line 130.

sentences.t: τὼ δ’ αὖτ’ ἐκ δίφρου γουναζέσθην·
sentences.l: and the two, on their side, from the chariot entreated him;
sentences.i: and the two, for their part, entreated him from the chariot:
sentences.n: τὼ δ’ αὖτ’ ‘and the two in turn’ goes back to the brothers (αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘again, on the other side’). γουναζέσθην is a dual imperfect of γουνάζομαι ‘entreat’; the verb is made from γόνυ ‘knee’, but ‘knees’ is not said. ἐκ δίφρου ‘from the chariot’ is where they still are. A speech follows.

sentences.t: ζώγρει Ἀτρέος υἱέ,
sentences.l: “Take alive, son of Atreus,
sentences.i: “Take us alive, son of Atreus,
sentences.n: ζώγρει is the present imperative of ζωγρέω ‘take alive’, and it has no object in the Greek. The speakers are the two brothers (the duals above), so `i` says ‘us’, where one man pleading says ‘take me alive’ elsewhere. Ἀτρέος υἱέ is the vocative υἱέ with the genitive Ἀτρέος (epic-Ionic, = Ἀτρέως), ‘son of Atreus’; Agamemnon is meant. The unit stops at the comma, in the middle of line 131.

sentences.t: σὺ δ’ ἄξια δέξαι ἄποινα·
sentences.l: and you accept worthy ransom;
sentences.i: and accept a ransom of full worth;
sentences.n: σὺ δ’ ‘and you’ turns the plea to Agamemnon. δέξαι is the aorist imperative middle of δέχομαι ‘accept’. ἄξια ‘worthy, of full worth’ is the neuter plural of ἄξιος and agrees with ἄποινα ‘ransom’, a plural noun for one payment. The unit stops at the raised dot, and its English is the one this half-line has where Adrestus begs in a similar way.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δ’ ἐν Ἀντιμάχοιο δόμοις κειμήλια κεῖται
χαλκός τε χρυσός τε πολύκμητός τε σίδηρος,
sentences.l:
Many treasures lie in the house of Antimachus,
bronze and gold and much-laboured iron,
sentences.i: In the house of Antimachus many treasures lie: bronze and gold and iron worked with much labour.
sentences.n: κειμήλια ‘treasures’ are things laid up in store; κεῖται is singular because a neuter plural takes a singular verb. The brothers name their own father in the third person, which tells Agamemnon whose house it is. δόμοις is a poetic plural and means ‘in the house’. χαλκός τε χρυσός τε πολύκμητός τε σίδηρος ‘bronze and gold and iron worked with much labour’ is a stock list, found in the Odyssey in the accusative; πολύκμητος comes from κάμνω ‘toil’. The unit stops at the comma.

sentences.t:
τῶν κέν τοι χαρίσαιτο πατὴρ ἀπερείσι’ ἄποινα,
εἰ νῶϊ ζωοὺς πεπύθοιτ’ ἐπὶ νηυσὶν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
of these our father would grant you unstinted ransom,
if us two alive he should learn of at the ships of the Achaeans.”
sentences.i: From these our father would grant you an unstinted ransom, if he were to learn that we two are alive at the ships of the Achaeans.”
sentences.n: τῶν κέν τοι χαρίσαιτο ‘of these he would grant you’: κέν with the aorist optative χαρίσαιτο (χαρίζομαι ‘grant as a favour’) is a potential, ‘would’, and τῶν is the partitive genitive ‘some of these’; τοι is ‘to you’. πατήρ is ‘father’ with the possessive left to be understood, ‘our’. ἀπερείσι’ is ἀπερείσια ‘unstinted’ (the house word), agreeing with ἄποινα ‘ransom’. εἰ … πεπύθοιτ’ ‘if he should learn’ is an aorist optative of πυνθάνομαι; νῶϊ is the dual accusative ‘we two’, and ζωούς ‘alive’ agrees with it. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς τώ γε κλαίοντε προσαυδήτην βασιλῆα
μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσιν·
sentences.l:
So the two of them, weeping, addressed the king
with gentle words;
sentences.i: So the two of them spoke to the king, weeping, with gentle words;
sentences.n: ὣς τώ γε ‘so those two’: τώ is a dual article used as a pronoun, and γε singles them out. κλαίοντε is the dual participle ‘weeping’ and προσαυδήτην the dual imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘address’. βασιλῆα ‘king’ is Agamemnon (the epic accusative -ῆα). μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσιν ‘with gentle words’ has the epic dative plurals -οις and -εσσιν, and is the stock phrase. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of line 137.

sentences.t: ἀμείλικτον δ’ ὄπ’ ἄκουσαν·
sentences.l: but an unsoftened voice they heard:
sentences.i: but the voice they heard was unyielding:
sentences.n: ἀμείλικτον ‘not to be softened’ is made from ἀ- and the root of μειλίσσω ‘soothe’, and answers μειλιχίοις ‘gentle’ earlier in the line: gentle words, a voice that does not give way. ὄπ’ is ὄπα, the accusative of ὄψ ‘voice’. ἄκουσαν is the aorist of ἀκούω without its augment (= ἤκουσαν), ‘they heard’. The voice is Agamemnon’s, and the speech follows.

sentences.t: εἰ μὲν δὴ Ἀντιμάχοιο δαΐφρονος υἱέες ἐστόν,
sentences.l: “If indeed of Antimachus, wise-minded, sons you two are,
sentences.i: “If you two are indeed the sons of wise-hearted Antimachus,
sentences.n: εἰ μὲν δή ‘if indeed’ opens a condition that is answered by νῦν μὲν δὴ … τίσετε in line 142; the relative clause in between tells what Antimachus did. ἐστόν is the dual of εἰμί, ‘you two are’, and υἱέες the epic nominative plural of υἱός. Agamemnon answers the brothers, and the quotation begins here.

sentences.t:
ὅς ποτ’ ἐνὶ Τρώων ἀγορῇ Μενέλαον ἄνωγεν
ἀγγελίην ἐλθόντα σὺν ἀντιθέῳ Ὀδυσῆϊ
αὖθι κατακτεῖναι μηδ’ ἐξέμεν ἂψ ἐς Ἀχαιούς,
sentences.l:
who once in the assembly of the Trojans bade Menelaus,
having come on news with godlike Odysseus,
there on the spot to kill him and not to let him go back to the Achaeans,
sentences.i: who once, in the assembly of the Trojans, bade Menelaus, when he had come with godlike Odysseus to bring news, to kill him on the spot and not to let him go back to the Achaeans,
sentences.n: ὃς ποτ’ ‘who once’ is a relative clause on Antimachus; ἐνὶ Τρώων ἀγορῇ is ‘in the assembly of the Trojans’ (ἐνί = ἐν, ἀγορῇ dative). ἄνωγεν ‘bade’ is the past of ἄνωγα, a perfect with present sense, and it governs two infinitives, κατακτεῖναι ‘to kill’ and μηδ’ ἐξέμεν ‘and not to let go’ (ἐξέμεν is the epic aorist infinitive of ἐξίημι), both with Μενέλαον as their object. ἐλθόντα is the aorist participle of ἔρχομαι, agreeing with Μενέλαον; ἀγγελίην ‘news’ is an accusative of purpose, ‘to bring news’, i.e. as envoy. ἀντιθέῳ is the stock ‘godlike’ and Ὀδυσῆϊ the epic dative of Ὀδυσσεύς. αὖθι is ‘there, on the spot’. The embassy is the one that Menelaus and Odysseus made to Troy and that Antenor tells of in Book 3.

sentences.t: νῦν μὲν δὴ τοῦ πατρὸς ἀεικέα τίσετε λώβην.
sentences.l: now then indeed for your father’s unseemly insult you shall pay.”
sentences.i: now you shall pay the penalty for your father’s unseemly insult.”
sentences.n: νῦν μὲν δή ‘now then’ answers the εἰ μὲν δή of line 138. τοῦ πατρός is ‘your father’s’: the article does the work of ‘your’. ἀεικέα ‘unseemly’ and λώβην ‘insult, outrage’ stand together, and τίσετε is the future of τίνω ‘pay’; the wrong done is what is paid for. The verb is a plural, ‘you shall pay’, where the dual would be τίσετον. The speech ends.

sentences.t:
ἦ, καὶ Πείσανδρον μὲν ἀφ’ ἵππων ὦσε χαμᾶζε
δουρὶ βαλὼν πρὸς στῆθος·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and Peisander from the horses thrust to the ground,
having struck him with a spear at the chest;
sentences.i: So he said, and struck Peisander on the chest with his spear and pushed him from his chariot to the ground;
sentences.n: ἦ, καί ‘he spoke, and’ closes the speech and starts the action. Πείσανδρον μέν is set against Ἱππόλοχος δέ in line 145. ἀφ’ ἵππων is ‘from the horses’, meaning off the chariot. ὦσε is the aorist of ὠθέω ‘push’ and χαμᾶζε ‘to the ground’ has the direction-ending -ζε. δουρί is the dative of δόρυ ‘spear’, βαλών the aorist participle ‘having struck’, and πρὸς στῆθος ‘at the chest’. The unit stops at the raised dot, in line 144.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ὕπτιος οὔδει ἐρείσθη.
sentences.l: and he on his back was driven to the ground.
sentences.i: and he was driven down on his back onto the ground.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is Peisander. ὕπτιος ‘on his back’ and ἐρείσθη, the aorist passive of ἐρείδω ‘press, drive’, with οὔδει ‘the ground’ in the dative, say that the spear-thrust drove him flat.

sentences.t: Ἱππόλοχος δ’ ἀπόρουσε,
sentences.l: And Hippolochus leapt down,
sentences.i: And Hippolochus leapt down,
sentences.n: Ἱππόλοχος δ’ ‘and Hippolochus’ answers the μέν of line 143. ἀπόρουσε is the aorist of ἀπορούω ‘leap away, leap off’; the Greek does not say off the chariot, but he is still in it. The unit stops at the comma, in line 145.

sentences.t:
τὸν αὖ χαμαὶ ἐξενάριξε
χεῖρας ἀπὸ ξίφεϊ τμήξας ἀπό τ’ αὐχένα κόψας,
sentences.l:
him in turn on the ground he despoiled,
having cut off with a sword the hands and having struck off the neck,
sentences.i: and him in turn he killed on the ground and stripped of his armour, cutting off his hands with his sword and striking off his neck,
sentences.n: τὸν αὖ ‘him in turn’; χαμαί ‘on the ground’ is the adverb of place (not χαμᾶζε ‘to the ground’). ἐξενάριξε is the aorist of ἐξεναρίζω ‘kill and strip of the armour’, from ἐνάρα ‘spoils’. χεῖρας ἀπὸ … τμήξας is ‘having cut off the hands’: ἀπό belongs to the participle (a tmesis), and τμήξας is the aorist participle of τμήγω ‘cut’. ἀπό τ’ αὐχένα κόψας is ‘and having struck off the neck’, κόψας from κόπτω. ξίφεϊ is the epic dative of ξίφος ‘sword’. The unit stops at the comma.

sentences.t: ὅλμον δ’ ὣς ἔσσευε κυλίνδεσθαι δι’ ὁμίλου.
sentences.l: and like a round block he sent him rolling, to be rolled through the throng.
sentences.i: and sent him rolling through the throng like a round block.
sentences.n: ὅλμον … ὣς ‘like a ὅλμος’ (ὣς after its noun): ὅλμος is something round that rolls, perhaps a boulder or a log; the object itself is not known, and ‘round block’ is a guess. ἔσσευε is the aorist of σεύω ‘make rush, send’; its object, Hippolochus’ body, is understood from the line before. κυλίνδεσθαι is the middle infinitive ‘to be rolled’; δι’ ὁμίλου is ‘through the throng’.

sentences.t: τοὺς μὲν ἔασ’·
sentences.l: These he left;
sentences.i: He left those two;
sentences.n: τοὺς μὲν ἔασ’ ‘these he left’: ἔασ’ is ἔασε, the aorist of ἐάω ‘let be, leave’, and τοὺς the two dead men. The μέν is answered by ὃ δ’ ‘but he’, who goes on to where the fighting is thickest. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of line 148.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ὅθι πλεῖσται κλονέοντο φάλαγγες,
τῇ ῥ’ ἐνόρουσ’, ἅμα δ’ ἄλλοι ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l:
and he, where most battle-lines were being thrown into confusion,
there he leapt in, and together with him the other well-greaved Achaeans.
sentences.i: and where the battle-lines were being thrown into confusion most, there he rushed in, and with him the other well-greaved Achaeans.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ὅθι … τῇ ῥ’ ἐνόρουσ’ ‘and he, where …, there he leapt in’: ὅθι ‘where’ is answered by τῇ ‘there’. πλεῖσται is the superlative of πολύς ‘most’, agreeing with φάλαγγες ‘battle-lines’; κλονέοντο is the imperfect passive of κλονέω ‘throw into confusion’. ἐνόρουσ’ is ἐνόρουσε, the aorist of ἐνορούω ‘leap in’. ἅμα δ’ ἄλλοι ‘and together with him others’; ἅμα is an adverb here. ἐϋκνήμιδες ‘well-greaved’ is the stock epithet of the Achaeans, and the edition prints the diaeresis.

sentences.t:
πεζοὶ μὲν πεζοὺς ὄλεκον φεύγοντας ἀνάγκῃ,
ἱππεῖς δ’ ἱππῆας·
sentences.l:
Men on foot were killing men on foot, fleeing under compulsion,
and horsemen horsemen;
sentences.i: Men on foot killed men on foot as they fled under compulsion, and horsemen killed horsemen;
sentences.n: πεζοὶ μὲν πεζούς … ἱππεῖς δ’ ἱππῆας sets the two arms of the army against each other in two matched pairs: πεζός ‘on foot’, ἱππεύς ‘horseman’ (ἱππῆας is the epic accusative plural). ὄλεκον is the unaugmented imperfect of ὀλέκω ‘destroy, kill’, a by-form of ὄλλυμι. φεύγοντας ἀνάγκῃ is ‘fleeing under compulsion’, ἀνάγκῃ the dative ‘by necessity’. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of line 151.

sentences.t:
ὑπὸ δέ σφισιν ὦρτο κονίη
ἐκ πεδίου, τὴν ὦρσαν ἐρίγδουποι πόδες ἵππων
χαλκῷ δηϊόωντες·
sentences.i: and beneath them dust rose from the plain, raised by the loud-crashing feet of horses wreaking havoc with bronze;
sentences.n: ὑπὸ δέ σφισιν ὦρτο κονίη ‘and from beneath them rose dust’: σφισιν is the epic dative ‘them’, ὑπό an adverb ‘from beneath’, and ὦρτο the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rise’. τὴν ὦρσαν ‘which they raised’: ὦρσαν is the transitive aorist of the same verb. ἐρίγδουποι ‘loud-crashing’ is the stock epithet (it is also Zeus’), and πόδες ἵππων ‘feet of horses’ is the subject. δηϊόωντες is a masculine plural participle of δηϊόω ‘cut down, ravage’ and agrees with πόδες; the feet stand for the riders, but the Greek does not say so. χαλκῷ is ‘with bronze’. The unit stops at the raised dot, in line 153.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
αἰὲν ἀποκτείνων ἕπετ’ Ἀργείοισι κελεύων.
sentences.l:
but lord Agamemnon
always killing followed, bidding the Argives.
sentences.i: but lord Agamemnon followed always killing, and giving orders to the Argives.
sentences.n: ἀτὰρ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων ‘but lord Agamemnon’ is the stock phrase. αἰέν is ‘always’. ἀποκτείνων ‘killing’ and κελεύων ‘giving orders’ are participles, the second with Ἀργείοισι ‘to the Argives’ in the epic dative -οισι. ἕπετ’ is ἕπετο ‘followed’, the imperfect of ἕπομαι, and has no object: he follows the fleeing Trojans.

sentences.t: ὡς δ’ ὅτε πῦρ ἀΐδηλον ἐν ἀξύλῳ ἐμπέσῃ ὕλῃ,
sentences.l: And as when a destroying fire in a dense woodland falls,
sentences.i: As when a destructive fire falls on dense woodland,
sentences.n: ὡς δ’ ὅτε … ἐμπέσῃ ‘and as when … falls’ opens a comparison; ἐμπέσῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ἐμπίπτω ‘fall upon’ after ὅτε. πῦρ ἀΐδηλον is ‘destroying fire’ in `l` and ‘destructive’ in `i`; ἀΐδηλος is either ‘destroying’ or ‘unseen’, and the first is chosen. ἀξύλῳ is not understood: by its parts it should mean ‘without wood’, which cannot go with ὕλῃ ‘woodland’, so the usual guess is that ἀ- is intensive, ‘very woody, dense’, and ‘dense’ is chosen in both layers. The unit stops at the comma.

sentences.t: πάντῃ τ’ εἰλυφόων ἄνεμος φέρει,
sentences.l: and everywhere, swirling, the wind carries it,
sentences.i: and the wind, swirling everywhere, carries it along,
sentences.n: πάντῃ ‘everywhere’, with generalising τ’. εἰλυφόων is a participle of εἰλυφάω ‘roll, swirl about’ (with the lengthened -όων), agreeing with ἄνεμος ‘wind’. φέρει ‘carries’ has the fire as its understood object; the simile is in the present, as in English.

sentences.t:
οἳ δέ τε θάμνοι
πρόρριζοι πίπτουσιν ἐπειγόμενοι πυρὸς ὁρμῇ·
sentences.l:
and the bushes
root and all fall, hard pressed by the rush of the fire;
sentences.i: and the bushes fall root and all, hard pressed by the rush of the fire;
sentences.n: οἳ δέ τε θάμνοι ‘and the bushes’: οἳ is the article, and τε generalises. πρόρριζοι ‘root and all’ is made from πρό ‘forward’ and ῥίζα ‘root’, torn up by the roots. πίπτουσιν is ‘fall’ and ἐπειγόμενοι ‘hard pressed’, the passive of ἐπείγω; πυρὸς ὁρμῇ is ‘by the onrush of the fire’, with the same noun as at 11.118. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ὑπ’ Ἀτρεΐδῃ Ἀγαμέμνονι πῖπτε κάρηνα
Τρώων φευγόντων,
sentences.l:
so then beneath Atreus’-son Agamemnon fell the heads
of the Trojans fleeing,
sentences.i: so, under Agamemnon, son of Atreus, the heads of the fleeing Trojans fell,
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ‘so then’ closes the comparison. ὑπ’ Ἀτρεΐδῃ Ἀγαμέμνονι is ‘beneath Agamemnon, son of Atreus’: ὑπό with the dative names the one under whose hand they fall, and Ἀτρεΐδῃ is the epic dative of Ἀτρεΐδης. πῖπτε is the unaugmented imperfect of πίπτω, taking up πίπτουσιν of the comparison; κάρηνα, the epic plural of κάρη, ‘heads’, stands for the men. Τρώων φευγόντων ‘of the Trojans fleeing’ is a genitive with its participle. The unit stops at the comma, in line 159.

sentences.t:
πολλοὶ δ’ ἐριαύχενες ἵπποι
κείν’ ὄχεα κροτάλιζον ἀνὰ πτολέμοιο γεφύρας
ἡνιόχους ποθέοντες ἀμύμονας·
sentences.i: and many strong-necked horses rattled empty chariots along the bridges of war, missing their blameless charioteers;
sentences.n: ἐριαύχενες ἵπποι ‘strong-necked horses’ is a stock phrase; the exact sense of ἐρι- is not known. κείν’ is κενά ‘empty’ (epic κεινός), and ὄχεα is the plural of ὄχος ‘chariot’, a Greek plural for one vehicle. κροτάλιζον is the imperfect of κροταλίζω ‘rattle, clatter’. ἀνὰ πτολέμοιο γεφύρας is ‘along the bridges of war’ (πτολέμοιο is the epic form of πολέμου): what γεφύρας means here is not known, and the same words stand at 8.378. ἡνιόχους ποθέοντες ἀμύμονας is ‘longing for their blameless charioteers’ (ποθέω ‘long for’, ἀμύμων ‘blameless’). The unit stops at the raised dot, in line 161.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἐπὶ γαίῃ
κείατο, γύπεσσιν πολὺ φίλτεροι ἢ ἀλόχοισιν.
sentences.l:
and they on the earth
lay, to vultures much dearer than to wives.
sentences.i: while the men lay on the ground, far dearer to vultures than to their wives.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘but they’ are the dead charioteers. κείατο is the epic imperfect of κεῖμαι ‘lie’. γύπεσσιν is the epic dative plural of γύψ ‘vulture’. πολὺ φίλτεροι ἢ ἀλόχοισιν is ‘much dearer than to wives’: the comparative φίλτεροι ‘dearer’ with ἢ, and the dative of the one they are dear to is understood from γύπεσσιν for the second half. ἄλοχος is ‘wife’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορα δ’ ἐκ βελέων ὕπαγε Ζεὺς ἔκ τε κονίης
ἔκ τ’ ἀνδροκτασίης ἔκ θ’ αἵματος ἔκ τε κυδοιμοῦ·
sentences.l:
But Hector out of the shafts Zeus led away, and out of the dust,
and out of the man-slaying, and out of the blood, and out of the tumult;
sentences.i: But Zeus drew Hector away from the shafts, out of the dust, out of the man-slaying, out of the blood, and out of the tumult;
sentences.n: ὕπαγε is the unaugmented imperfect of ὑπάγω ‘lead away from under’. The five ἐκ-phrases (the first is ἐκ βελέων) say what he is led out of: βελέων ‘shafts’ (βέλος), κονίης ‘dust’, ἀνδροκτασίης ‘man-slaying’ (the Odyssey’s word too), αἵματος ‘blood’ and κυδοιμοῦ ‘tumult’, the noise and uproar of battle. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t: Ἀτρεΐδης δ’ ἕπετο σφεδανὸν Δαναοῖσι κελεύων.
sentences.l: but Atreus’-son followed furiously, bidding the Danaans.
sentences.i: while the son of Atreus followed furiously, giving orders to the Danaans.
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδης δ’ ‘but the son of Atreus’ turns from Hector back to Agamemnon. ἕπετο is ‘followed’, with σφεδανόν ‘furiously’ (σφεδανός is ‘impetuous’; here the neuter used as an adverb); κελεύων ‘giving orders’ takes the epic dative Δαναοῖσι ‘to the Danaans’. The poet moves from Argives to Danaans without a change of meaning.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ παρ’ Ἴλου σῆμα παλαιοῦ Δαρδανίδαο
μέσσον κὰπ πεδίον παρ’ ἐρινεὸν ἐσσεύοντο
ἱέμενοι πόλιος·
sentences.i: And they were rushing past the tomb of old Ilus, Dardanus’ descendant, through the middle of the plain and past the wild fig tree, eager for the city;
sentences.n: οἳ δὲ … ἐσσεύοντο ‘and they were rushing’: οἳ δέ are the Trojans, and ἐσσεύοντο is the imperfect of σεύομαι ‘rush’. παρ’ Ἴλου σῆμα παλαιοῦ Δαρδανίδαο is ‘past the tomb of old Ilus, Dardanus’ descendant’: σῆμα, a marker, is the house ‘tomb’, and Δαρδανίδαο the epic genitive of Δαρδανίδης ‘descendant of Dardanus’. μέσσον κὰπ πεδίον is ‘through the middle of the plain’, κὰπ being κατά with its last letter taken over by the π of πεδίον. παρ’ ἐρινεόν ‘past the wild fig tree’ is a landmark. ἱέμενοι πόλιος ‘eager for the city’ takes the genitive (πόλιος is the epic form of πόλεως). The unit stops at the raised dot, in line 168.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ κεκλήγων ἕπετ’ αἰεὶ
Ἀτρεΐδης,
sentences.l:
and he, shouting, followed always,
Atreus’-son,
sentences.i: and the son of Atreus followed always, with a shrill cry,
sentences.n: ὃ δὲ κεκλήγων ‘and he, shouting’ is Agamemnon, named by Ἀτρεΐδης at the start of the next line, which the unit therefore takes in. κεκλήγων is the perfect participle of κλάζω ‘shriek, cry’, and ‘with a shrill cry’ is the English. ἕπετ’ αἰεί is ‘followed always’. The unit stops at the comma, in line 169.

sentences.t: λύθρῳ δὲ παλάσσετο χεῖρας ἀάπτους.
sentences.l: and with gore he was spattered, as to the hands, untouchable.
sentences.i: and his irresistible hands were spattered with gore.
sentences.n: λύθρῳ ‘with gore’ is the dative of λύθρον, blood mixed with dirt after fighting. παλάσσετο is the imperfect passive of παλάσσω ‘spatter’. χεῖρας ἀάπτους is an accusative of respect, ‘as to his hands’ (so `i` makes the hands the subject). ἄαπτος is not understood; two traditional guesses are ‘untouchable’ and ‘irresistible’, and `l` takes the first, `i` the second.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ Σκαιάς τε πύλας καὶ φηγὸν ἵκοντο,
sentences.l: But when they reached the Scaean Gates and the oak,
sentences.i: But when they reached the Scaean Gates and the oak,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ‘but when’ takes ἵκοντο, the unaugmented aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘reach’. Σκαιὰς … πύλας is ‘the Scaean Gates’, a name kept as a name; φηγόν is ‘an oak’, here a landmark on the plain. The unit stops at the comma.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ ἄρα δὴ ἵσταντο καὶ ἀλλήλους ἀνέμιμνον.
sentences.l: there then indeed they halted and waited for one another.
sentences.i: there they halted and waited for one another.
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ ἄρα δή ‘there then indeed’ marks the end of the flight. ἵσταντο is the imperfect middle of ἵστημι, ‘took their stand, halted’, and ἀνέμιμνον the imperfect of ἀναμένω ‘wait for’ (ἀλλήλους ‘one another’).

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἔτι κὰμ μέσσον πεδίον φοβέοντο βόες ὥς,
sentences.l: But they still through the middle of the plain were fleeing in terror like cattle,
sentences.i: but the rest were still in flight through the middle of the plain, like cattle,
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ἔτι ‘but they still’ are the Trojans who have not yet reached the gates. κὰμ μέσσον πεδίον is κατὰ μέσσον πεδίον, with the κατά taking on the μ of μέσσον. φοβέοντο is the imperfect passive of φοβέω, ‘were put to flight, were fleeing in terror’ (the epic -έοντο). βόες ὥς ‘like cattle’ begins a comparison, with ὥς after its noun. The unit stops at the comma, and the comparison runs on.

sentences.t:
ἅς τε λέων ἐφόβησε μολὼν ἐν νυκτὸς ἀμολγῷ
πάσας·
sentences.l:
which a lion has put to flight, coming in the dark of night,
all of them;
sentences.i: that a lion puts to flight when he comes in the dark of night, all of them;
sentences.n: ἅς τε … ἐφόβησε ‘which … puts to flight’: ἅς is the relative on βόες, with generalising τε. ἐφόβησε is an aorist of the kind used for what happens every time, so the English uses the present. μολών is the aorist participle of βλώσκω ‘go, come’. νυκτὸς ἀμολγῷ is ‘in the ἀμολγός of night’: the sense of ἀμολγός is not known (ancient guesses are ‘milking-time’ and ‘darkness’), and ‘dark of night’ is a guess. πάσας ‘all of them’ is in line 174 but belongs with ἐφόβησε. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of line 174.

sentences.t: τῇ δέ τ’ ἰῇ ἀναφαίνεται αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος·
sentences.l: and to one of them steep destruction appears;
sentences.i: and for one of them steep destruction appears;
sentences.n: τῇ δέ τ’ ἰῇ ‘and to one’: ἰῇ is epic for μιᾷ ‘one’ (here one cow out of the herd), and τε generalises. ἀναφαίνεται is ‘shows itself, appears’. αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος is the stock ‘steep destruction’, destruction coming as from a height. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
τῆς δ’ ἐξ αὐχέν’ ἔαξε λαβὼν κρατεροῖσιν ὀδοῦσι
πρῶτον,
sentences.l:
and of her from out the neck he breaks, having seized it with strong teeth,
first,
sentences.i: first he seizes her in his strong teeth and breaks her neck,
sentences.n: τῆς δ’ ‘and of her’ is the one cow. ἐξ … ἔαξε is a tmesis for ἐξέαξε ‘breaks out, breaks’, from ἄγνυμι; αὐχέν’ is αὐχένα ‘neck’; λαβών is ‘having seized’; κρατεροῖσιν ὀδοῦσι is ‘with strong teeth’, in the epic dative plural -οισιν, ὀδούς being ‘tooth’. ἔαξε is the same kind of aorist as ἐφόβησε, so the English is present. πρῶτον ‘first’, at the head of line 176, opens the order of the meal, which ἔπειτα ‘then’ continues. The unit stops at the comma, after the first word of line 176.

sentences.t: ἔπειτα δέ θ’ αἷμα καὶ ἔγκατα πάντα λαφύσσει·
sentences.l: and then blood and all the entrails he gulps down;
sentences.i: and then he gulps down the blood and all the entrails;
sentences.n: ἔπειτα δέ θ’ ‘and then’ (θ’ is the generalising τε). αἷμα καὶ ἔγκατα πάντα is ‘the blood and all the entrails’, and λαφύσσει is the present of λαφύσσω ‘gulp down, devour’. The unit stops at the raised dot, which ends the comparison.

sentences.t:
ὣς τοὺς Ἀτρεΐδης ἔφεπε κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
αἰὲν ἀποκτείνων τὸν ὀπίστατον·
sentences.l:
so them Atreus’-son pursued, lord Agamemnon,
always killing the hindmost;
sentences.i: So the son of Atreus, lord Agamemnon, pursued them, always killing the hindmost;
sentences.n: ὣς τοὺς … ἔφεπε ‘so he pursued them’: ἔφεπε is the imperfect of ἐφέπω ‘pursue’, and τοὺς are the Trojans. Ἀτρεΐδης … κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων gives the stock names in full. ἀποκτείνων ‘killing’ takes τὸν ὀπίστατον ‘the hindmost’, the superlative of ὀπίσσω ‘behind’: whoever is last at that moment. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of line 178.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἐφέβοντο.
sentences.l: and they were fleeing.
sentences.i: and they fled.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are the Trojans. ἐφέβοντο is the imperfect of φέβομαι ‘flee’. This short unit closes the sentence.

sentences.t:
πολλοὶ δὲ πρηνεῖς τε καὶ ὕπτιοι ἔκπεσον ἵππων
Ἀτρεΐδεω ὑπὸ χερσί·
sentences.l:
And many, face down and on their backs, fell out of the horses
under the hands of Atreus’-son;
sentences.i: and many, face down and on their backs, fell from their chariots beneath the hands of the son of Atreus;
sentences.n: πρηνεῖς τε καὶ ὕπτιοι ‘face down and on their backs’ gives both ways a man can fall (πρηνής ‘face down’, ὕπτιος ‘on the back’). ἔκπεσον is the aorist of ἐκπίπτω ‘fall out’, and ἵππων, ‘of the horses’, means out of the chariots. Ἀτρεΐδεω is the epic genitive of Ἀτρεΐδης (-εω = -ου); ὑπὸ χερσί is ‘beneath the hands’, with the epic dative plural χερσί. The unit stops at the raised dot, in line 180.

sentences.t: περὶ πρὸ γὰρ ἔγχεϊ θῦεν.
sentences.l: for far ahead with the spear he raged.
sentences.i: for he raged with his spear far in front.
sentences.n: περὶ πρὸ γάρ ‘for …’ gives the reason for the many falls. The pair περὶ πρό is not understood: περί can mean ‘exceedingly’ and πρό ‘forward’, and ‘far ahead’ is a guess. θῦεν is the imperfect of θύω ‘rage, rush’, and ἔγχεϊ is the epic dative of ἔγχος ‘spear’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τάχ’ ἔμελλεν ὑπὸ πτόλιν αἰπύ τε τεῖχος
ἵξεσθαι,
sentences.l:
But when indeed soon he was about, under the city and the steep wall,
to come,
sentences.i: But when he was on the point of coming up under the city and its steep wall,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ‘but when’ opens a time clause answered by τότε δή in the next unit. ἔμελλεν ‘was about to’ takes the future infinitive ἵξεσθαι ‘to come, reach’, with Agamemnon understood as subject, and τάχ’ is τάχα ‘soon’. ὑπὸ πτόλιν αἰπύ τε τεῖχος is ‘up under the city and the steep wall’: πτόλις is the old form of πόλις, αἰπύς ‘steep’ is the stock word for a wall, and ὑπό with the accusative is ‘up to the foot of’. The unit stops at the comma, after the first word of line 182.

sentences.t:
τότε δή ῥα πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε
Ἴδης ἐν κορυφῇσι καθέζετο πιδηέσσης
οὐρανόθεν καταβάς·
sentences.i: then the father of men and of gods sat down on the peaks of Ida with its many springs, having come down from heaven;
sentences.n: τότε δή ῥα ‘then indeed’ answers ὅτε in the unit before. πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε is the stock ‘father of men and of gods’ (Zeus), subject of καθέζετο ‘sat down’. Ἴδης … κορυφῇσι is ‘on the peaks of Ida’, κορυφῇσι the epic dative plural, and πιδηέσσης ‘with many springs’ (from πίδαξ ‘spring’) agrees with Ἴδης. οὐρανόθεν ‘from heaven’ has -θεν ‘from’, and καταβάς is ‘having come down’. The unit stops at the raised dot, in line 184.

sentences.t: ἔχε δ’ ἀστεροπὴν μετὰ χερσίν.
sentences.l: and he held lightning in his hands;
sentences.i: and he held a flash of lightning in his hands;
sentences.n: ἔχε δ’ ‘and he held’ is the unaugmented imperfect of ἔχω. ἀστεροπήν is ‘lightning’, the flash; it is the noun that the stock ἀστεροπητής ‘lightning-flasher’ is made from. μετὰ χερσίν is ‘in his hands’, μετά with the dative. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t: Ἶριν δ’ ὄτρυνε χρυσόπτερον ἀγγελέουσαν·
sentences.l: and Iris he urged on, gold-winged, to tell the news;
sentences.i: and he urged gold-winged Iris on to bring news:
sentences.n: Ἶριν δ’ ὄτρυνε ‘and he urged Iris on’: ὄτρυνε is the aorist of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’. χρυσόπτερον ‘gold-winged’ is the stock epithet of Iris. ἀγγελέουσαν is the future participle (of purpose) of ἀγγέλλω ‘announce’, ‘to bring news’. The line also stands at 8.398, where Zeus sends the same messenger, and its English is kept. A speech follows.

sentences.t: βάσκ’ ἴθι Ἶρι ταχεῖα, τὸν Ἕκτορι μῦθον ἐνίσπες·
sentences.l: “Go, set out, swift Iris, this word to Hector tell;
sentences.i: “Be off with you, swift Iris, and give Hector this word:
sentences.n: βάσκ’ ἴθι is a pair of imperatives, ‘go, set out’ (βάσκε elided, and ἴθι from εἶμι), the usual way Zeus sends a messenger. Ἶρι ταχεῖα is the vocative ‘swift Iris’; ταχεῖα is from ταχύς ‘swift’. τὸν … μῦθον is ‘this word’: τόν points forward to what Zeus is about to say. Ἕκτορι is ‘to Hector’, and ἐνίσπες is the aorist imperative of ἐνέπω ‘tell’. The unit stops at the raised dot. Zeus speaks.

sentences.t:
ὄφρ’ ἂν μέν κεν ὁρᾷ Ἀγαμέμνονα ποιμένα λαῶν
θύνοντ’ ἐν προμάχοισιν ἐναίροντα στίχας ἀνδρῶν,
sentences.l:
As long as he sees Agamemnon, shepherd of the people,
rushing among the front-fighters, slaying the ranks of men,
sentences.i: As long as he sees Agamemnon, shepherd of the people, charging among the foremost fighters and slaying the ranks of men,
sentences.n: ὄφρ’ ἂν μέν κεν ὁρᾷ ‘as long as he sees’: ὄφρα with ἄν and κεν, both marking the condition, and the present subjunctive ὁρᾷ of ὁράω. Ἀγαμέμνονα ποιμένα λαῶν is the stock ‘Agamemnon, shepherd of the people’. θύνοντ’ ‘rushing’ (θύνω) and ἐναίροντα ‘slaying’ (ἐναίρω) are participles agreeing with Ἀγαμέμνονα. ἐν προμάχοισιν is ‘among the front-fighters’, the foremost men, and στίχας is the accusative plural ‘ranks’. The unit stops at the comma; the clause with τόφρα ‘for so long’ comes next.

sentences.t: τόφρ’ ἀναχωρείτω,
sentences.l: for that long let him step back,
sentences.i: for that long let him step back,
sentences.n: τόφρ’ ἀναχωρείτω ‘for that long let him step back’: τόφρα answers the ὄφρα of the unit before, and ἀναχωρείτω is a third-person imperative, ‘let him withdraw’. Zeus speaks to Iris about Hector, so he says ‘let him’, not ‘you’. The unit stops at the comma, in line 189.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἄλλον λαὸν ἀνώχθω
μάρνασθαι δηΐοισι κατὰ κρατερὴν ὑσμίνην.
sentences.l:
and the rest of the people let him bid
to fight against the enemy throughout the strong battle.
sentences.i: and let him tell the rest of the army to fight the enemy throughout the strong battle.
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ἄλλον λαόν ‘and the rest of the people’ (λαός is ‘army’ in `i`, as for a force in the field). ἀνώχθω is the third-person imperative of ἄνωγα ‘bid’, a perfect with present sense: ‘let him bid’. μάρνασθαι is ‘to fight’; δηΐοισι is the dative plural of δήϊος ‘hostile’, used as a noun, ‘the enemy’; κατὰ κρατερὴν ὑσμίνην is ‘throughout the strong battle’, the house phrase for hard fighting.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί κ’ ἢ δουρὶ τυπεὶς ἢ βλήμενος ἰῷ
εἰς ἵππους ἅλεται,
sentences.l:
But when either struck by a spear or hit by an arrow
into his horses he leaps,
sentences.i: But when, struck by a spear or hit by an arrow, he leaps into his chariot,
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεί κ’ ‘but when’ is ἐπεί with κε and the subjunctive. ἢ … ἢ … ‘either … or’ joins δουρὶ τυπείς ‘struck by a spear’ (τυπείς is the aorist passive participle of τύπτω) and βλήμενος ἰῷ ‘hit by an arrow’ (βλήμενος is the aorist middle participle of βάλλω; ἰῷ is the dative of ἰός ‘arrow’). εἰς ἵππους ἅλεται is ‘leaps into his horses’, meaning into his chariot, ἅλεται being the aorist subjunctive of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’. The unit stops at the comma, in line 192.

sentences.t:
τότε οἱ κράτος ἐγγυαλίξω
κτείνειν εἰς ὅ κε νῆας ἐϋσσέλμους ἀφίκηται
δύῃ τ’ ἠέλιος καὶ ἐπὶ κνέφας ἱερὸν ἔλθῃ.
sentences.l:
then to him strength I will put into his hands
to kill, until he reaches the well-benched ships
and the sun sets and sacred darkness comes on.”
sentences.i: then I will put strength into his hands to kill, until he reaches the well-benched ships and the sun sets and sacred darkness comes on.”
sentences.n: τότε οἱ κράτος ἐγγυαλίξω ‘then I will put strength into his hands’: οἱ is ‘to him’, κράτος is ‘strength’ (the house word), and ἐγγυαλίξω is the future of ἐγγυαλίζω ‘put into the hands’. κτείνειν is ‘to kill’; εἰς ὅ κε … ἀφίκηται is ‘until he reaches’ (the subjunctive with κε), with νῆας ἐϋσσέλμους ‘the well-benched ships’. δύῃ τ’ ἠέλιος is ‘and the sun sets’, and ἐπὶ κνέφας ἱερὸν ἔλθῃ is ‘and sacred darkness comes on’: ἐπί is an adverb, κνέφας ‘darkness’ is neuter, and ἱερόν ‘sacred’ is said of the dark as it is elsewhere of the day. Zeus’ speech ends.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε ποδήνεμος ὠκέα Ἶρις,
sentences.l: So he spoke, and did not disobey, wind-footed, swift Iris,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Iris, wind-footed and swift, did not disobey;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes the speech (ἔφατ’ is ἔφατο, from φημί). οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε is ‘and did not disobey’ (ἀπιθέω is the opposite of πείθομαι ‘obey’). ποδήνεμος ὠκέα Ἶρις names the subject, last in the Greek: ποδήνεμος ‘wind-footed’ and ὠκέα ‘swift’ are her stock epithets.

sentences.t: βῆ δὲ κατ’ Ἰδαίων ὀρέων εἰς Ἴλιον ἱρήν.
sentences.l: and she went down from the Idaean mountains to sacred Ilium.
sentences.i: and she went down from the Idaean mountains to sacred Ilium.
sentences.n: βῆ δέ ‘and she went’ (βῆ is ἔβη, the aorist of βαίνω). κατ’ Ἰδαίων ὀρέων is ‘down from the Idaean mountains’, κατά with the genitive. εἰς Ἴλιον ἱρήν is ‘to sacred Ilium’: ἱρήν is the Ionic form of ἱεράν, and Ilium is Troy.

sentences.t:
εὗρ’ υἱὸν Πριάμοιο δαΐφρονος Ἕκτορα δῖον
ἑσταότ’ ἔν θ’ ἵπποισι καὶ ἅρμασι κολλητοῖσιν·
sentences.l:
She found the son of Priam, wise-minded, heavenly Hector,
standing among horses and well-joined chariot;
sentences.i: She found the son of wise-hearted Priam, heavenly Hector, standing among his horses and well-joined chariot;
sentences.n: εὗρ’ is εὗρε, ‘found’. υἱὸν Πριάμοιο δαΐφρονος Ἕκτορα δῖον is ‘the son of Priam, wise-minded, heavenly Hector’: δαΐφρονος goes with Πριάμοιο, δῖον ‘heavenly’ with Ἕκτορα, and Ἕκτορα stands beside υἱόν to name him. ἑσταότ’ is the perfect participle of ἵστημι, ‘standing’ (ἑσταότα with its last vowel elided). ἔν θ’ ἵπποισι καὶ ἅρμασι κολλητοῖσιν is ‘among horses and well-joined chariots’: ἔν ‘among’, and the plural ἅρμασι stands for the one chariot; κολλητός is ‘well-joined’, literally ‘glued’. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη προσέφη πόδας ὠκέα Ἶρις·
sentences.l: And standing close by, swift-in-feet Iris spoke;
sentences.i: Iris, swift of foot, came and stood close by, and spoke;
sentences.n: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη προσέφη ‘and standing close by she spoke’ is the usual way Iris begins a message. πόδας ὠκέα Ἶρις is ‘Iris, swift of foot’, πόδας an accusative of respect, ‘as to her feet’. The line is the same as at 2.790, and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ υἱὲ Πριάμοιο Διὶ μῆτιν ἀτάλαντε
Ζεύς με πατὴρ προέηκε τεῒν τάδε μυθήσασθαι.
sentences.l:
“Hector, son of Priam, to Zeus in cunning equal,
Zeus the father sent me forth to you these things to tell.
sentences.i: “Hector, son of Priam, the equal of Zeus in cunning, father Zeus has sent me to tell you this:
sentences.n: Ἕκτορ υἱὲ Πριάμοιο are vocatives, ‘Hector, son of Priam’. Διὶ μῆτιν ἀτάλαντε is ‘equal to Zeus in cunning’: ἀτάλαντε is the vocative of ἀτάλαντος ‘equal’ with the dative Διί, and μῆτιν, ‘cunning’, is an accusative of respect. Ζεύς με πατήρ is ‘Zeus the father … me’; προέηκε is the aorist of προΐημι ‘send forth’, τεΐν the epic dative ‘to you’ (= σοί), τάδε ‘these things’, and μυθήσασθαι ‘to tell’ an infinitive of purpose. Iris speaks, and what she says repeats Zeus’ message in the lines that follow.

sentences.t:
ὄφρ’ ἂν μέν κεν ὁρᾷς Ἀγαμέμνονα ποιμένα λαῶν
θύνοντ’ ἐν προμάχοισιν, ἐναίροντα στίχας ἀνδρῶν,
sentences.l:
As long as you see Agamemnon, shepherd of the people,
rushing among the front-fighters, slaying the ranks of men,
sentences.i: As long as you see Agamemnon, shepherd of the people, charging among the foremost fighters and slaying the ranks of men,
sentences.n: These two lines repeat 187–188, as a messenger repeats the words he was given, with ὁρᾷς ‘you see’ in place of ὁρᾷ ‘he sees’; the English follows the earlier unit with ‘you’. The unit stops at the comma.

sentences.t: τόφρ’ ὑπόεικε μάχης,
sentences.l: for that long give way from the fighting,
sentences.i: for that long give way from the fighting,
sentences.n: τόφρ’ ὑπόεικε μάχης ‘for that long give way from the fight’: ὑπόεικε is the imperative of ὑπείκω ‘give way, yield’, and μάχης is a genitive of separation. In Zeus’ message the same place had ἀναχωρείτω ‘let him step back’: Iris puts the order to Hector himself with a different verb. The unit stops at the comma, in line 204.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἄλλον λαὸν ἄνωχθι
μάρνασθαι δηΐοισι κατὰ κρατερὴν ὑσμίνην.
sentences.l:
and the rest of the people bid
to fight against the enemy throughout the strong battle.
sentences.i: and tell the rest of the army to fight the enemy throughout the strong battle.
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ἄλλον λαὸν ἄνωχθι ‘and bid the rest of the people’: ἄνωχθι is the imperative of ἄνωγα ‘bid’, where Zeus’ message had the third person ἀνώχθω ‘let him bid’. The rest is as at 189–190: μάρνασθαι ‘to fight’, δηΐοισι ‘the enemy’, κατὰ κρατερὴν ὑσμίνην ‘throughout the strong battle’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί κ’ ἢ δουρὶ τυπεὶς ἢ βλήμενος ἰῷ
εἰς ἵππους ἅλεται,
sentences.l:
But when either struck by a spear or hit by an arrow
into his horses he leaps,
sentences.i: But when, struck by a spear or hit by an arrow, he leaps into his chariot,
sentences.n: The same words as 191–192, here with the same Greek: ἐπεί κ’ with the subjunctive ἅλεται ‘when he leaps’, δουρὶ τυπείς ‘struck by a spear’ and βλήμενος ἰῷ ‘hit by an arrow’, εἰς ἵππους ‘into his horses’, i.e. into his chariot. The unit stops at the comma, in line 207.

sentences.t:
τότε τοι κράτος ἐγγυαλίξει
κτείνειν, εἰς ὅ κε νῆας ἐϋσσέλμους ἀφίκηαι
δύῃ τ’ ἠέλιος καὶ ἐπὶ κνέφας ἱερὸν ἔλθῃ.
sentences.l:
then to you strength he will put into your hands
to kill, until you reach the well-benched ships
and the sun sets and sacred darkness comes on.”
sentences.i: then he will put strength into your hands to kill, until you reach the well-benched ships and the sun sets and sacred darkness comes on.”
sentences.n: τότε τοι κράτος ἐγγυαλίξει ‘then he will put strength into your hands’: τοι is ‘to you’, and ἐγγυαλίξει is third person, because Iris reports what Zeus promised (Zeus himself said ἐγγυαλίξω ‘I will put’). εἰς ὅ κε … ἀφίκηαι is ‘until you reach’, in the second person for Hector. The last line is as at 194. Iris’ speech ends.

sentences.t: ἣ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ἀπέβη πόδας ὠκέα Ἶρις,
sentences.l: She, indeed, then so having spoken went away, swift-in-feet Iris,
sentences.i: So she spoke, and Iris, swift of foot, went away;
sentences.n: ἣ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ‘she, then, having so spoken’ closes a speech: ἣ is the article as a pronoun, and εἰποῦσ’ is εἰποῦσα, the aorist participle of λέγω. ἀπέβη is ‘went away’ (ἀποβαίνω, aorist), and πόδας ὠκέα Ἶρις is ‘Iris, swift of foot’. The line is the same as at 8.425, and its English is kept.

sentences.t: Ἕκτωρ δ’ ἐξ ὀχέων σὺν τεύχεσιν ἆλτο χαμᾶζε,
sentences.l: and Hector from the chariot, with his armour, leapt to the ground,
sentences.i: and Hector leapt from his chariot to the ground in his armour,
sentences.n: Ἕκτωρ δ’ ‘and Hector’. ἐξ ὀχέων σὺν τεύχεσιν is ‘from the chariot, with his armour’: ὄχεα is the plural for one chariot, and τεύχεσιν the dative plural of τεύχεα ‘armour’. ἆλτο is the aorist of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’, and χαμᾶζε ‘to the ground’. A line like this stands at 5.494, with αὐτίκα ‘at once’ in place of Ἕκτωρ.

sentences.t:
πάλλων δ’ ὀξέα δοῦρα κατὰ στρατὸν ᾤχετο πάντῃ
ὀτρύνων μαχέσασθαι, ἔγειρε δὲ φύλοπιν αἰνήν.
sentences.l:
and brandishing sharp spears he went through the army everywhere,
urging them to fight, and he roused fearsome battle-din.
sentences.i: and brandishing sharp spears he went everywhere through the army, urging the men to fight, and he roused fearsome battle-din.
sentences.n: πάλλων is ‘brandishing’ (πάλλω ‘shake’) with ὀξέα δοῦρα ‘sharp spears’; κατὰ στρατὸν ᾤχετο is ‘went through the army’ (ᾤχετο is the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘go’), πάντῃ ‘everywhere’. ὀτρύνων ‘urging’ takes the aorist infinitive μαχέσασθαι ‘to fight’. ἔγειρε is ‘roused’ (ἐγείρω ‘wake, rouse’), with φύλοπιν αἰνήν, the stock ‘fearsome battle-din’. These two lines stand also at 5.495–496.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἐλελίχθησαν καὶ ἐναντίοι ἔσταν Ἀχαιῶν,
sentences.l: And they were whirled round and stood opposite the Achaeans,
sentences.i: They wheeled round and took their stand facing the Achaeans,
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are the Trojans, rallied by Hector. ἐλελίχθησαν is the aorist passive of ἐλελίζω ‘whirl round’, here ‘wheeled about’. ἐναντίοι ἔσταν Ἀχαιῶν is ‘stood opposite the Achaeans’: ἔσταν is ἔστησαν, the intransitive aorist of ἵστημι, with ἐναντίοι ‘opposite’ and the genitive Ἀχαιῶν. The line is also 5.497, where a different line follows.

sentences.t: Ἀργεῖοι δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἐκαρτύναντο φάλαγγας.
sentences.l: and the Argives, from the other side, made strong their battle-lines.
sentences.i: and the Argives on the other side strengthened their battle-lines.
sentences.n: Ἀργεῖοι δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ‘and the Argives from the other side’ sets the Achaean army against the Trojans, under the second of its three names. ἐκαρτύναντο is the aorist middle of καρτύνω ‘make strong’ (from κράτος), and φάλαγγας ‘battle-lines’ is the accusative plural of φάλαγξ.

sentences.t: ἀρτύνθη δὲ μάχη, στὰν δ’ ἀντίοι·
sentences.l: And the battle was set in order, and they stood opposite one another;
sentences.i: and the battle was set in order, and they stood facing one another;
sentences.n: ἀρτύνθη δὲ μάχη ‘and the battle was set in order’: ἀρτύνθη is the aorist passive of ἀρτύνω ‘arrange’, so the lines are drawn up. στὰν δ’ ἀντίοι is ‘and they stood facing’: στὰν is ἔστησαν, and ἀντίοι ‘facing’; the subject, the two armies, is understood. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of line 216.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ Ἀγαμέμνων
πρῶτος ὄρουσ’,
sentences.l:
and in, Agamemnon
first leapt,
sentences.i: and Agamemnon was the first to leap in,
sentences.n: ἐν δ’ … ὄρουσ’ is a tmesis for ἐνόρουσε ‘leapt in’; ὄρουσ’ is ὄρουσε, the aorist of ὀρούω ‘rush, leap’, with Ἀγαμέμνων as subject, and πρῶτος ‘first’ says he was ahead of the rest. The unit stops at the comma, in line 217.

sentences.t: ἔθελεν δὲ πολὺ προμάχεσθαι ἁπάντων.
sentences.l: and he wished far to fight in front of all.
sentences.i: and he wished to fight far in front of them all.
sentences.n: ἔθελεν δέ ‘and he wished’ is the unaugmented imperfect of ἐθέλω. προμάχεσθαι is ‘to fight in front’ (the verb of προμάχοι ‘front-fighters’), with πολύ ‘by far’ and the genitive ἁπάντων ‘of all’, ‘before them all’.

sentences.t: ἔσπετε νῦν μοι Μοῦσαι Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχουσαι·
sentences.l: Tell now to me, Muses, who hold the Olympian halls
sentences.i: Tell me now, Muses, you who hold the halls of Olympus:
sentences.n: ἔσπετε νῦν μοι Μοῦσαι ‘tell me now, Muses’ is the poet’s call for help, the same words as at 2.484. ἔσπετε is the aorist imperative of ἐνέπω, ‘tell’ (an old form with -σπ-). Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχουσαι is ‘who hold the Olympian halls’, a feminine participle. The question it asks is in the two lines that follow.

sentences.t:
ὅς τις δὴ πρῶτος Ἀγαμέμνονος ἀντίον ἦλθεν
ἢ αὐτῶν Τρώων ἠὲ κλειτῶν ἐπικούρων.
sentences.l:
who indeed first came against Agamemnon,
of the Trojans themselves or of the famous allies.
sentences.i: who it was that first came against Agamemnon, whether of the Trojans themselves or of their famous allies.
sentences.n: ὅς τις δή ‘who, indeed’ opens an indirect question, ‘who it was that’. ἦλθεν is ‘came’, and ἀντίον ‘against, facing’ takes the genitive Ἀγαμέμνονος. ἢ αὐτῶν Τρώων ἠὲ κλειτῶν ἐπικούρων is ‘either of the Trojans themselves or of the famous allies’, with ἠέ answering ἤ; κλειτῶν ‘famous’ (= κλυτῶν) and ἐπικούρων ‘allies’ are the house words. The Muses’ answer comes in the next part.
